chunks: "Sampling is taking a continuous signal and recording its value only at regular instants, say every T s seconds, so I end up with a list of numbers instead of a curve.
In an ADC, that's the sample-and-hold grabbing the voltage on a capacitor at each clock edge. What matters is what that costs you.
If the signal is band-limited and I sample at more than twice its highest frequency, no information is lost: in principle I can reconstruct the original exactly.
That's the Nyquist criterion. If I sample too slowly, frequencies above half the sample rate fold back down and look like lower frequencies.
A 900 hertz tone sampled at 1 kilohertz looks exactly like a 100 hertz tone. Once it's sampled, you can't tell them apart.
So in practice I put a low-pass anti-alias filter in front of the ADC and sample comfortably faster than twice my bandwidth, usually five to ten times, so the filter can be simple.
I also keep in mind that sampling is separate from quantization. Sampling discretizes time; quantization discretizes amplitude.
And the clock needs to be clean, because timing jitter converts directly into amplitude noise on fast signals."
